newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Gunmen seize Japanese in Philippine beach resort.
newsitem.headline: Gunmen seize Japanese in Philippine beach resort.

text.p: Gunmen seized a Japanese businessman on a beach in the southern Philippines and shot dead his Filipino companion in the latest of a wave of abductions, police said on Monday.
News of the abduction broke as President Fidel Ramos was leaving Manila on a nine-day trip to Britain, Greece and Oman to try to attract foreign investors.

Six armed men, after shooting dead the Filipino, took away Kenichi Takayama and five other Filipinos on Sunday while they having a beach party in a resort in Glan town, Sarangani island, 1,120 km (695 miles) southeast of Manila.
Pursuing troops killed one of the gunmen in a shootout later but Takayama's fate was not immediately known, police said.

A police official said the armed men could have originally planned to rob the group, but decided to take hostages after killing one of them, a Filipino engineer. The kidnappers fled into the rugged hills in Sarangani island.
Takayama is registered as a resident of nearby General Santos city, a fledgling business district in southern Mindanao island, hesaid.
A Japanese embassy official said the embassy was still trying to confirm who the Japanese victim was, noting there were three versions of his name, all of them fairly common.
In Manila, officials of the watchdog Citizens Action Against Crime (CAAC) said the latest of a series of kidnappings in the country could hurt business confidence.

"Before, the concern of investors has been whether or not foreign nationals are being kidnapped. They didn't seem to care if the kidnap victims were not foreigners," CAAC spokeswoman Tess Baltazar told Reuters.
"I think incidents like this will affect business. It creates instability and an environment not conducive to investors."
Japan is the Philippines' third largest foreign investor and largest aid donor.
Kidnap-for-ransom has become a booming trade in a country Fortune Magazine has dubbed "Asia's kidnap capital." Police said the label was unfair.
The southern Philippines, home to bandits and Moslem separatist rebels, is especially notorious for its kidnappings.

At least 89 people have been kidnapped around the country in the first four months of this year with gangs collecting 152 million pesos ($5.7 million) in ransom from victims' relatives, statistics compiled by citizens' groups showed.
The amount more than doubled that collected by kidnappers for all of last year when they got at least 69 million pesos in ransom from families of 241 kidnap victims.
In 1995, kidnap gangs seized 199 people and collected at least 112 million pesos in ransom, the citizens' groups said.

Takayama was the first Japanese abducted in the country since two Filipino soldiers kidnapped a construction firm owner in Manila in January 1994. He was freed after payment of seven million pesos in ransom.
Another Japanese, Nobuyki Wakaoji, then a director at Mitsui and Co Ltd, was the victim in one of the country's biggest kidnapping cases.
Abducted in 1986, Wakaoji was released months later after payment of $3 million ransom. Two Filipino masterminds of the kidnapping were sentenced to life imprisonment in 1992.
Widespread belief that soldiers and police protect kidnappers has discouraged Filipinos from reporting to the authorities.

Kidnapping incidents have continued despite President Ramos's order to the military last month to take over the job of hunting down the gangs, saying the army had more firepower to fight them. (Conversion $ = 26.3)
